cues.text: A Boy of the Fields
Francisco Marto was born on June 11, 1908 , in Aljustrel, the sixth of seven children of Manuel and Olímpia Marto and older brother to Jacinta , not yet two when she arrived.
He was a gentle, easygoing boy who loved animals more than competition, catching lizards and once giving away his only penny to set a caged bird free.
He played a simple reed pipe while his sister and cousin sang and danced beside him, and rarely quarreled even when treated unfairly.
His father later said Francisco was the more courageous of the two children, willing to walk alone through the dark countryside at night without a flicker of fear.
Nothing about this quiet shepherd boy marked him out as anything but ordinary.
Yet it was precisely this stillness, this readiness to be overlooked, that Heaven seemed to choose.
The Angel's Silence
In 1916, the year before Our Lady herself appeared, Francisco and his companions reported three visits from an angel who taught them to pray and to make sacrifices for sinners.
Even here his path differed quietly from theirs; something in Francisco always leaned toward silence rather than words.
He accepted what Lúcia told him of the angel's message and began praying the Rosary with an earnestness unusual in so young a boy.
A soul does not need to hear every word to be changed by what it has encountered.
Francisco's whole life would prove that stillness itself can be a form of listening.
Seeing Without Hearing
When the Lady appeared at the Cova da Iria beginning on May 13, 1917 , Francisco alone among the three children could see her but never hear her voice.
He depended on Lúcia to tell him afterward what had been said.
It might have left a lesser soul feeling shut out.
Instead, simply beholding her seemed to satisfy something in him that words could not have reached.
Lúcia later described a boy transformed all the same, drawn ever more inward toward what he came to call "the Hidden Jesus."
Even a Lady he could not hear was enough to lead him, wordlessly, straight to her Son.
Held Under Threat, Then Vindicated
That August, Francisco was seized along with his sister and cousin and threatened with execution by boiling oil unless he denied what he had seen.
He held his silence rather than tell a lie, and was released once the threat failed to break the children's testimony.

By the final apparition that October, some seventy thousand people had gathered in a rain-soaked field to witness what became known as the Miracle of the Sun, Francisco among them, as quietly amazed as everyone else.
Courage, in Francisco, never looked like defiance.
It looked like a boy simply refusing to say what was not true, and trusting Our Lady with the rest.
Consoling the Hidden Jesus
After the apparitions ended, Francisco was sent to school but preferred, whenever he could manage it, to stay behind in the parish church instead.
He would tell Lúcia to go on without him, and spend the whole day kneeling before the tabernacle.
There he kept company with a God he had come to see as quietly sorrowful over the sins of the world.
Asked once what he wanted to be when he grew up, Francisco answered simply that he wanted to be nothing at all, only to die and go to Heaven.
His devotion to the Eucharist never competed with his love for Our Lady.
The two were, for him, a single current, since it was she who had first led him to the tabernacle and taught him to love what he found there.
To console Jesus, for Francisco, and to love His Mother, were never two different tasks.
A Quiet Death
On December 23, 1918 , Francisco came down with bronchial pneumonia, the same illness that would soon claim his sister too.
Sensing his death was near, he told those nursing him he would soon see Heaven, adding that once there he would console Jesus and Our Lady a great deal.
He bore the sickness through a hard winter without a single complaint, saying it seemed so small a thing beside all he still hoped to offer God.
On the morning of April 4, 1919 , having received Holy Communion as Viaticum the day before, Francisco died quietly at home at the age of ten.
A faint smile, witnesses said, was still on his face.
Legacy: Contemplate Like Francisco
Francisco Marto was beatified with Jacinta on May 13, 2000, and canonized on May 13, 2017, on the hundredth anniversary of that first apparition.
Pope John Paul II, at their beatification, captured the two children's spirituality in a phrase still repeated at Fátima: "to contemplate like Francisco and love like Jacinta."
It suits him perfectly.
Where his sister could not stop speaking her love aloud, Francisco showed his simply by staying, hour after hour, in a silence that asked nothing and adored everything.
We live in a noisier world than his, one that rarely rewards a child who wants to be nothing more than present to God.
Francisco's short life suggests that such presence, quietly offered to Jesus and to the Mother who led him there, may be the greatest offering of all.
